The Wyoming toad Anaxyrus baxteri is a critically endangered amphibian endemic to the Laramie Basin of southeastern Wyoming, and its life history has been inferred from closely related bufonids due to the extreme rarity of wild populations. At a constant water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the larval period from hatching through metamorphic climax extends for approximately 40 days , a developmental duration that aligns closely with the timetable reported for the common toad Bufo bufo under equivalent thermal regimes. Newly metamorphosed toadlets emerge from the water at a remarkably small body size, with wet weight at birth recorded at just 0.07 grams [Wwb = just 0.07 grams], a mass that reflects the minimal yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva before the onset of exogenous feeding. This modest neonatal mass imposes a considerable physiological challenge, as the recently metamorphosed juvenile must immediately begin foraging on small invertebrates to fuel its subsequent growth trajectory in the semi-arid shortgrass prairie habitat that defines the species natural range.

Following the terrestrial transition, post-metamorphic juveniles enter a period of rapid mass gain that ultimately culminates in the attainment of adult body dimensions. Field measurements and captive rearing studies indicate that the maximum recorded adult mass in the Wyoming toad is approximately 40 grams [Wwi = approximately 40 grams], a value that is modest relative to other members of the genus Anaxyrus but consistent with the energetic constraints of a high-elevation environment with a short active season. This ultimate wet weight is achieved through several years of sustained feeding on ants, beetles, and other arthropods, with growth rates heavily influenced by the availability of prey and the duration of the summer foraging window. The relatively small adult body size of this species likely reflects an evolutionary trade-off, as a reduced mass permits earlier maturation and higher reproductive output within the constraints of a harsh climate where winters force prolonged brumation and a corresponding cessation of feeding activity.

Reproductive activity in the Wyoming toad is tightly synchronized with spring snowmelt and the formation of ephemeral breeding ponds, a pattern that concentrates egg deposition into a narrow temporal window. Females produce approximately 900 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 900 eggs per clutch] and typically produce only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] when water temperatures reach 15 °C [T = 15 °C], reflecting the physiological capacity for oocyte production under favorable thermal conditions. The clutch itself is deposited as a gelatinous string containing several thousand eggs, which are attached to submerged vegetation in shallow water where solar warming accelerates embryonic development and reduces the duration of the vulnerable egg stage.

The onset of sexual maturation in this species is a protracted process that follows the completion of somatic growth, with puberty occurring at approximately 2.5 years following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 2.5 years following metamorphosis] under the thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This extended juvenile period is typical of many montane anurans, as the short growing season at high elevation limits annual mass gain and delays the attainment of the minimum body size required for gonadal development. Males tend to reach maturity slightly earlier than females, though the difference is marginal and both sexes typically require at least two full active seasons before they become capable of amplexus and successful reproduction. The relatively late age at maturity is a critical demographic vulnerability for the Wyoming toad, as it means that any perturbation reducing juvenile survival during the long pre-reproductive phase can have disproportionately severe effects on population persistence.

Longevity records for the Wyoming toad are limited due to the species precipitous decline, but comparative data from other Anaxyrus species in the AnAge database suggest a maximum lifespan of 13 years [am = 13 years] when individuals are maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This substantial longevity potential, which spans well over a decade in ideal conditions, is somewhat unusual for a small-bodied anuran and may reflect the slow pace of life characteristic of high-latitude amphibians that experience a prolonged period of seasonal inactivity each winter. In the wild, however, most individuals likely succumb to predation, disease, or habitat desiccation long before reaching physiological senescence. The chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis has been particularly devastating, causing catastrophic population crashes that reduced the species to just a handful of individuals in the 1990s and necessitating intensive captive breeding efforts that now form the backbone of all current conservation programs.
